KEY MESSAGE 1... Drier and cooler this afternoon and overnight as 
deepening low pressure continues to move away. 

Visible satellite shows pockets of stratocumulus clouds indicative 
of ongoing strong low and mid level cold air advection this 
afternoon. Another indicator is the stiff west breeze that will 
continue this afternoon as mixing heights rise to >3 kft and tap 
into a 35-40 kt LLJ. Model soundings show a well-mixed PBL overnight 
and so expect lows to remain a bit warmer than they otherwise could 
be. Lows tonight likely remain above freezing, ranging from the mid 
30s inland to the low to mid 40s across coastal areas. Greatest 
chance of better decoupling and cooler temperatures will be found 
across interior valleys where lows may dip into the lower 30s early 
Monday morning. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Cloudy and unsettled start to the workweek as 
multiple weak disturbances move through.

We remain under WNW flow with another upper level trough clearing 
the region through Monday night, and with it cooler temperatures 
prevail aloft. 850 mb temperatures look to fall below 0C late Monday 
night then steadily improve through the day on Tuesday to around 2- 
4C. These cooler conditions aloft will remain supportive of a mix of 
clouds and sunshine. Guidance has trended towards more in the way of 
isolated to scattered showers Monday afternoon as low level lapse 
rates steepen to 8-9 C/km. Best forcing for ascent will be found 
across NW Massachusetts so expecting scattered coverage of showers 
there and isolated coverage elsewhere. Highs Monday and Tuesday look 
to be generally in the 40s and 50s with lows in the 30s. These more 
seasonable temperatures are expected to continue through at least 
midweek as the WNW to W flow aloft continues. Breezy conditions at 
the surface are expected at least for Tuesday as another low looks 
to pass to our northeast.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Monitoring potential storminess late this week into 
part of the weekend, with lower elevation rain and higher elevation 
rain mixing with wet snow possible.

Model-ensembles and AI-based guidance continue to point to potential 
late-week / early-weekend storminess. However these models continue 
to vary on the placement, strength and eventual exit of the modeled 
surface low; as well as the thermal structure and more specifically, 
the extent to which sub-freezing air aloft can penetrate into 
Southern New England. A lead shortwave disturbance coming out of the 
north-central Rockies Tue moves into the central Plains around early 
Wed; then the 500 mb CONUS pattern amplifies substantially as strong 
Pacific trough energy induces amplifying upper ridging across the 
Rockies by midweek. Strong northerly 500 mb flow then helps allow 
for additional pieces of shortwave energy coming out of the northern 
Canadian Prairies/northern Canada to dig southward and/or 
potentially phase with the Rockies trough around Thursday/Thursday 
night. It's a complicated interaction and how those pieces come 
together are critical in terms of resolving the above described 
uncertainties. The net result is a deep upper trough/closed low at 
500 mb located somewhere in the OH/TN Valleys; and an organizing 
surface low moving northward from the mid-Atlantic states Thursday 
night, and over or in vicinity of Southern New England around 
Friday, with lingering influence possibly into the upcoming weekend.

Latest guidance indicates that sub-freezing air aloft could struggle 
to make it into Southern New England at least initially, only then 
slowly bleeding into interior higher terrain areas in Southern New 
England late Friday night and/or into Saturday, possibly 
facilitating a rain to a gloppy wet snow changeover in the higher 
terrain. Lower elevations and the coastal plain seem more favored to 
stay as primarily rain due to both above-freezing air aloft and the 
influx of "milder" onshore flow of maritime air (SSTs still in the 
mid 50s). The GFS-based guidance has shown a westward/inland trend 
over the past few cycles which is a warmer and wetter outcome. The 
international guidance is closer to the 40N/70W benchmark or even 
further east, which would bring colder air in sooner but would in 
turn also be more removed from the best moisture/modeled QPF. 
Highest ensemble probabilities for an inch or more of snow at a 10:1 
SLR across the interior higher terrain are still in the moderate 
range at around 40-60% and are less than 20% for snow totals of 3 or 
more inches. 

Still is time to reassess the guidance, and continued variation in 
the guidance is likely over the coming days, at least until the lead 
shortwave becomes better resolved as it comes out of the Rockies 
around Tuesday.
